papers.title: "It Listens Better Than My Therapist": Exploring Social Media Discourse on LLMs as Mental Health Tool
papers.abstract: The emergence of generative AI chatbots such as ChatGPT has prompted growing public and academic interest in their role as informal mental health support tools. While early rule-based systems have been around for several years, large language models (LLMs) offer new capabilities in conversational fluency, empathy simulation, and availability. This study explores how users engage with LLMs as mental health tools by analyzing over 10,000 TikTok comments from videos referencing LLMs as mental health tools. Using a self-developed tiered coding schema and supervised classification models, we identify user experiences, attitudes, and recurring themes. Results show that nearly 20% of comments reflect personal use, with these users expressing overwhelmingly positive attitudes. Commonly cited benefits include accessibility, emotional support, and perceived therapeutic value. However, concerns around privacy, generic responses, and the lack of professional oversight remain prominent. It is important to note that the user feedback does not indicate which therapeutic framework, if any, the LLM-generated output aligns with. While the findings underscore the growing relevance of AI in everyday practices, they also highlight the urgent need for clinical and ethical scrutiny in the use of AI for mental health support.

papers.title: Foundations of GenIR
papers.abstract: The chapter discusses the foundational impact of modern generative AI models on information access (IA) systems. In contrast to traditional AI, the large-scale training and superior data modeling of generative AI models enable them to produce high-quality, human-like responses, which brings brand new opportunities for the development of IA paradigms. In this chapter, we identify and introduce two of them in details, i.e., information generation and information synthesis. Information generation allows AI to create tailored content addressing user needs directly, enhancing user experience with immediate, relevant outputs. Information synthesis leverages the ability of generative AI to integrate and reorganize existing information, providing grounded responses and mitigating issues like model hallucination, which is particularly valuable in scenarios requiring precision and external knowledge. This chapter delves into the foundational aspects of generative models, including architecture, scaling, and training, and discusses their applications in multi-modal scenarios. Additionally, it examines the retrieval-augmented generation paradigm and other methods for corpus modeling and understanding, demonstrating how generative AI can enhance information access systems. It also summarizes potential challenges and fruitful directions for future studies.

papers.title: Reframing Ethical Governance of Artificial Intelligence in Mental Health Care: Toward a Human-Centered, Explainable, and Clinically Responsible Psychotherapeutic Paradigm
papers.abstract: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into Mental Health care represents a transformative shift in the diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment of psychological disorders. While AI-driven tools—including digital phenotyping systems, natural language processing models, and conversational agents—offer significant potential to enhance diagnostic precision, accessibility, and personalized interventions, they simultaneously introduce complex ethical, clinical, and epistemological challenges. This study provides a comprehensive and critical synthesis of contemporary literature (2019–2025) to examine the ethical implications of AI deployment in psychotherapeutic contexts. Moving beyond descriptive review, the paper develops a conceptual ethical governance framework grounded in the principles of autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice, as well as the emerging “ethics of care” paradigm. It identifies key risk domains, including algorithmic bias, opacity of decision-making processes, data privacy vulnerabilities, erosion of therapeutic alliance, and the reconfiguration of professional accountability. Furthermore, the study proposes a human-centered, explainable, and clinically supervised AI integration model, emphasizing transparency, continuous ethical auditing, stakeholder inclusion, and hybrid human–AI decision-making structures. The findings highlight that while AI can significantly improve efficiency and expand access to mental healthcare—particularly in resource-constrained settings—its unregulated or poorly designed application may exacerbate inequalities, compromise patient autonomy, and undermine trust in clinical practice. The paper contributes to the interdisciplinary discourse by offering a structured ethical framework that bridges technological innovation with clinical responsibility and humanistic values. It concludes that sustainable and ethically aligned AI integration in mental health requires robust regulatory architectures, cross-disciplinary collaboration, and the preservation of the fundamentally human dimensions of psychotherapy.

papers.title: A Systematic Review on Artificial Intelligence-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems in Depression
papers.abstract: Purpose: This systematic review examines the current landscape of artificial intelligence (AI)-based Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) designed to aid in the treatment of depression. With depression recognized as a complex and multifactorial condition, often differing across contexts such as postpartum, adolescence, and elderly populations, the review aims to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and potential of AI-based CDSS in supporting personalized care. The primary research question explores how these systems are implemented and evaluated in clinical settings, as well as the main challenges to their broader adoption.Methods: The review analyzed studies focused on AI-based CDSS for depression, identifying variations in algorithms, performance metrics, and implementations. Studies were assessed based on system purposes, categorized into treatment selection, prediction and risk assessment, and clinical support and data review, providing a comprehensive overview of each study’s approach and outcomes.Results: 11 unique algorithms, 9 performance metrics, and 10 CDSS implementations were identified across the studies. Findings indicate positive results for CDSS in supporting clinical decision-making, yet highlight challenges in applying these tools in routine practice. Limitations include small, non-diverse sample sizes, immature methodologies, and difficulties in workflow integration, along with concerns about data privacy and the ethical use of AI.Conclusions: AI-based CDSS for depression shows potential in patient care; however, foundational issues such as more diverse samples and robust model development remain critical. Addressing these aspects will set the stage for future research into advanced applications, such as virtual-reality integration and multi-condition prediction, thus advancing AI’s role in mental health treatment.Clinical Relevance—This work illustrates the state of art of AI adoption in the domain of mental health, specifically in the context of depression.

papers.title: The application of AI-assisted music therapy tools in mental health interventions
papers.abstract: With the rising prevalence of mental health problems across populations, the limitations of traditional interventions have become more evident. Music therapy has received growing attention as a psychological intervention, and recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have created new opportunities for this field. This review examines the application potential and implementation pathways of AI-assisted music therapy tools for mental health interventions. Drawing on the literature and representative cases, this review summarizes application models and reported effects of AI in music therapy. The available evidence suggests that AI-assisted music therapy tools can support personalized interventions by adapting to users’ emotional and psychological states. Reported benefits include reductions in anxiety and depressive symptoms and improvements in emotion regulation across groups such as children, adolescents, and older adults. Finally, this review outlines priorities for future translation into mental health services and emphasizes data privacy and ethical standards to ensure responsible deployment.

literature_themes.summary: This cluster explores the use of AI, particularly large language models and clinical decision support systems, in mental health interventions. Key findings include positive user attitudes towards LLMs for emotional support and accessibility, but concerns about privacy and lack of professional oversight. AI-based CDSS show potential in personalized depression treatment, while ethical frameworks emphasize human-centered, explainable AI. AI-assisted music therapy also demonstrates benefits in reducing anxiety and depression.
literature_themes.limitations: Common limitations include lack of therapeutic framework alignment in LLM outputs, algorithmic bias, opacity in decision-making, data privacy vulnerabilities, erosion of therapeutic alliance, and need for ethical standards. Studies often rely on self-reported data or small samples, and generalizability across populations is limited.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster highlights gaps in integrating AI with established therapeutic frameworks, ensuring explainability and clinical responsibility, and addressing privacy and bias. It supports identifying research opportunities for developing human-centered, ethically governed AI tools that complement traditional therapy and are validated across diverse populations.

literature_themes.theme: Foundations of Generative AI for Information Access
literature_themes.summary: This cluster focuses on how generative AI models, through large-scale training and superior data modeling, transform information access systems. It introduces two key paradigms: information generation (creating tailored content) and information synthesis (integrating existing information to reduce hallucination). The chapter covers foundational aspects like architecture, scaling, training, and applications in multi-modal scenarios, including retrieval-augmented generation.
literature_themes.limitations: The cluster may not fully address challenges such as model hallucination in complex domains, scalability issues in real-time applications, or the trade-offs between generation quality and computational cost. It also lacks empirical evaluations across diverse tasks.
literature_themes.gap_relevance: This cluster provides a theoretical foundation for identifying gaps in generative IR, such as the need for robust evaluation metrics, methods to ensure factual accuracy in synthesis, and efficient integration of external knowledge sources. It highlights opportunities for improving retrieval-augmented generation and multi-modal information access.

summary: The literature highlights AI's potential in mental health through tools like LLMs for emotional support, CDSS for depression, and AI-assisted music therapy, with benefits in accessibility and personalization. However, key challenges include privacy, bias, lack of clinical oversight, and integration with therapeutic frameworks, underscoring the need for human-centered, explainable, and ethically governed AI systems.
gap: Despite the recognized potential of AI tools in mental health, there is a lack of empirical studies that systematically evaluate the integration of AI-generated outputs with established therapeutic frameworks (e.g., cognitive-behavioral therapy) to ensure clinical validity and therapeutic alignment, while also addressing privacy, bias, and explainability in diverse populations.
question: How can AI-generated mental health support be aligned with established therapeutic frameworks like cognitive-behavioral therapy to ensure clinical validity, and what are the impacts on therapeutic outcomes, user trust, and ethical considerations across diverse populations?
hypothesis: Integrating AI-generated cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) suggestions into a digital mental health intervention, compared to standard AI-generated support without CBT alignment, will result in significantly greater reductions in depression and anxiety symptoms, higher user trust, and lower perceived bias among diverse populations.
methodology: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) will compare an AI chatbot delivering CBT-aligned responses (experimental group) against a standard AI chatbot without CBT alignment (control group) over 8 weeks. Participants (N=300) with mild-to-moderate depression/anxiety will be recruited from diverse demographics via online platforms. Primary outcomes include symptom reduction (PHQ-9, GAD-7), user trust (Trust in AI Scale), and perceived bias (adapted scale). Secondary outcomes measure therapeutic alliance (WAI-SR) and adherence. Validity risks (e.g., attrition, self-report bias) will be mitigated through intent-to-treat analysis, randomization, and blinding of assessors. Scope is limited to CBT alignment; other frameworks are excluded.
proposal: AI tools in mental health, such as large language models and clinical decision support systems, show promise for improving accessibility and personalization, yet no randomized controlled trial (RCT) has compared AI-generated support aligned with a therapeutic framework like cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) versus non-aligned AI. Existing studies (e.g., Haensch, 2025; Chiang et al., 2025) evaluate standalone AI tools without systematic alignment to clinical protocols, raising concerns about clinical validity, user trust, and ethical risks such as bias and privacy. This study addresses the gap by asking: How can AI-generated mental health support be aligned with CBT to ensure clinical validity, and what are the impacts on therapeutic outcomes, user trust, and ethical considerations across diverse populations? We hypothesize that an AI chatbot delivering CBT-aligned responses (via a fine-tuned LLM with CBT-specific prompts and a rule-based safety layer) will yield significantly greater reductions in depression and anxiety symptoms (PHQ-9, GAD-7), higher user trust (Trust in AI Scale), and lower perceived bias (adapted scale) compared to a standard AI chatbot without CBT alignment, with effects moderated by demographic diversity. A two-arm RCT (N=300, powered at 80% to detect a moderate effect, d=0.4) over 8 weeks will compare the CBT-aligned chatbot against a non-aligned chatbot (baseline: generic empathetic responses). Primary outcomes are symptom reduction, trust, and perceived bias; secondary outcomes include therapeutic alliance (WAI-SR) and adherence. Novelty lies in empirically testing CBT alignment via a fine-tuned LLM, whereas prior work (e.g., Wei & He, 2026) focuses on AI tools without therapeutic grounding. Expected contributions include evidence-based guidelines for designing clinically valid AI interventions and insights into trust and bias mitigation, advancing human-centered, ethically governed AI. Key limitations include reliance on self-report, potential attrition (mitigated by intent-to-treat analysis and multiple imputation), and focus on CBT only; ethical safeguards include crisis detection protocols and human oversight.
draft_proposal: AI tools in mental health, such as large language models and clinical decision support systems, show promise for improving accessibility and personalization, yet their integration with established therapeutic frameworks like cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) remains understudied. Existing research focuses on standalone AI applications without systematic alignment to clinical protocols, raising concerns about clinical validity, user trust, and ethical risks such as bias and privacy. This study addresses the gap by asking: How can AI-generated mental health support be aligned with CBT to ensure clinical validity, and what are the impacts on therapeutic outcomes, user trust, and ethical considerations across diverse populations? We hypothesize that an AI chatbot delivering CBT-aligned responses will yield greater reductions in depression and anxiety symptoms, higher user trust, and lower perceived bias compared to standard AI support. A randomized controlled trial (N=300) over 8 weeks will compare CBT-aligned versus non-aligned AI chatbots, measuring symptom reduction (PHQ-9, GAD-7), trust (Trust in AI Scale), and perceived bias. This proposal extends prior work by empirically testing CBT integration, whereas existing studies often evaluate AI tools without therapeutic grounding. Expected contributions include evidence-based guidelines for designing clinically valid AI interventions and insights into user trust and bias mitigation, advancing human-centered, ethically governed AI in mental health.

proposal_critique.clarity_issues: The problem definition is clear but could be more precise by explicitly stating the lack of empirical studies aligning AI outputs with CBT. The phrase 'remains understudied' is vague; specify the gap as 'no RCT has compared CBT-aligned vs. non-aligned AI chatbots.'
proposal_critique.logic_issues: The logic flows from gap to question to hypothesis to methodology, but the hypothesis does not explicitly mention 'diverse populations' as in the question. Also, the expected contributions mention 'bias mitigation' but the methodology only measures perceived bias, not actual bias reduction.
proposal_critique.novelty_issues: The novelty is moderate: testing CBT alignment is a logical next step, but the idea of aligning AI with CBT is not entirely new. The proposal could be strengthened by specifying a novel CBT-alignment algorithm or a unique population (e.g., adolescents, low-resource settings).
proposal_critique.methodology_issues: The RCT design is feasible but lacks detail on how CBT alignment will be operationalized (e.g., rule-based vs. fine-tuned LLM). The sample size of 300 is adequate but power analysis is missing. Attrition and self-report bias are mentioned but not fully addressed (e.g., no plan for missing data beyond ITT).
proposal_critique.literature_alignment_issues: The proposal aligns well with Theme 1 (AI in mental health) and cites relevant papers, but it does not explicitly reference Paper 2 (GenIR foundations) which could inform the technical design of the AI chatbot. The gap statement could better integrate limitations from the literature (e.g., lack of therapeutic framework alignment from Paper 1).
proposal_critique.academic_depth_issues: The proposal lacks theoretical grounding in CBT principles (e.g., which specific CBT techniques will be used). It also does not discuss potential mechanisms (e.g., why CBT alignment improves trust). The ethical considerations are mentioned but not deeply explored (e.g., how to handle crisis situations).
proposal_critique.revision_plan: Strengthen the problem definition by explicitly stating the lack of RCTs comparing CBT-aligned vs. non-aligned AI. Add a power analysis and details on CBT operationalization (e.g., using a fine-tuned LLM with CBT-specific prompts). Include a theoretical framework linking CBT alignment to trust and outcomes, and discuss ethical safeguards for crisis detection.

rubric_scores.justification: The research problem (lack of CBT-aligned AI support), motivation (gaps in clinical validity, trust, bias), background (AI tools in mental health), target users (mild-to-moderate depression/anxiety), and proposed solution (CBT-aligned chatbot) are exceptionally clear. Implications for clinical practice and ethical design are explicitly discussed.

The proposal logically flows from literature analysis to gap identification (no RCT on CBT alignment), hypothesis generation, method design (RCT with two arms), and evaluation planning. Each stage is mutually supportive, with clear inputs/outputs.

The proposal is meaningfully distinct: it empirically tests CBT alignment via fine-tuned LLM, whereas prior work (e.g., Haensch, Chiang, Wei) evaluates AI tools without systematic therapeutic grounding. The contribution is methodological (CBT-aligned LLM) and evaluative (RCT on outcomes, trust, bias).

The RCT design is realistic with clear sample size (N=300, powered), comparison groups, primary/secondary outcomes, and risk mitigation (intent-to-treat, blinding). However, details on fine-tuning the LLM (e.g., data source, cost) and crisis detection protocols could be more specific.

The proposal is strongly grounded in retrieved papers: it cites Haensch (2025) on LLM discourse, Chiang et al. (2025) on CDSS, Wei & He (2026) on music therapy, and the ethical framework paper. It accurately identifies gaps (lack of therapeutic alignment) and explains how the proposal extends prior work.

The proposal demonstrates mature academic thinking: verifiable assumptions (hypothesis based on literature), theoretical awareness (CBT framework), methodological rigor (RCT, validated scales), and limitation awareness (self-report, attrition, focus on CBT only). It moves beyond summarization to research-level insight.
Writing is clear, concise, and professional. Sections are well organized, terminology is consistent, and the proposal is easy to follow. Citations are appropriately used.

evaluation.comments: The proposal is exceptionally clear, logically coherent, novel, feasible, and well-grounded in literature. It demonstrates PhD-level depth and is presented professionally. Minor refinements in implementation details would enhance feasibility further.
